title: DOT-MoE: Differentiable Optimal Transport for MoEfication
claim: Performance improves with finer-grained experts until saturation, and sparser training generalizes better to extreme sparsity, while throughput stays stable.
layout: 3 panels in a row: line plot, two-line plot, grouped bar chart
description: A single row of three plots, each with a lettered caption underneath. Panel (a), Expert Granularity, is a blue line plot of WikiText perplexity against number of experts (16 to 256). Perplexity drops steeply from about 26 to 20.5 and then flattens, with a light shaded area under the curve. Panel (b), Effect of training sparsity, plots accuracy against inference FFN sparsity (90% down to 30%). A red line for a model trained at 75% sparsity sits above a blue line for one trained at 50% sparsity. Star markers highlight each line's own training sparsity. Panel (c), Inference Throughput, is a grouped bar chart of throughput (K tok/s) for E=8, 16, 74 and 148 experts. Each group has three bars for batch sizes 1024, 2048 and 4096, in blue, teal and green. The bars are nearly equal in height. The eye goes first to the steep drop in (a) and the red-over-blue gap in (b). A footnote about results from other papers is cropped in at the top.
caption: Ablation results for \name. (a) Increasing expert granularity improves performance until saturation. (b) Training with higher FFN sparsity yields robust expert representations that generalize better to extreme sparsity regimes at inference time. (c) Inference throughput remains stable across expert granularities when active parameters are held constant.
abstract: The scaling of Large Language Models (LLMs) has driven significant performance gains but created substantial challenges in inference efficiency. While Mixture of Experts (MoEs) architectures address this by decoupling model size from inference cost, training MoEs from scratch is often unstable and compute intensive. Conversion of pre-trained dense models into sparse MoEs has emerged as an alternative solution; however, existing methods typically rely on heuristic neuron clustering or random splitting to partition the Feed-Forward Network (FFN) into experts. In this work, we propose DOT-MoE, a novel framework that formulates the decomposition of dense layers as a Differentiable Optimal Transport (DOT) problem. Instead of static heuristics, we model neuron assignment as a balanced transport problem, utilizing differentiable Sinkhorn-Knopp iterations to enforce strict expert capacity constraints. Furthermore, we utilize Straight-Through Estimators (STE) to jointly learn the discrete neuron-to-expert assignment and the token-to-expert routing policy end-to-end. Extensive experiments across multiple architectures and benchmarks demonstrate that DOT-MoE significantly outperforms structured pruning, heuristic clustering, and random-split baselines, retaining 90% of the original dense model's performance while reducing active parameters by 50%.
